text: Joseph told his brothers, "Tell my father of all my glory." The secret of worship is telling the Father about His Son.
explanation:
Nothing delights the Father more than His Son. No one ever loved God with all his heart, soul, mind and strength the way Jesus did, and when He came up from the waters of baptism, heaven opened: "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

So when you worship, sing to the Father about Jesus. Talk to Him about His Son. And what you do with the Son is what the Father does with you: love His Son, and the Father loves you; accept His Son, and you're accepted. Angels never tire of worshipping Him. He doesn't need our worship; we need to give it. It's what we were made for.

text: "Be filled with the Spirit, speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs." All three are singing.
explanation:
In the Greek, "be filled" is a present command: keep on being filled. And the way Paul describes it is remarkably simple: singing. Psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, "singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord." Praying in the Spirit belongs here too.

You don't need a church service. Sing in the shower, under your breath on the way to work, or on the drive to the hospital to visit someone. It's very hard to sing to the Lord and stay depressed. By the time you arrive, you'll find yourself full of the Spirit, with His wisdom ready for whatever is waiting.

text: Bible hope isn't "I hope so." Elpis is a confident, certain expectation of good in your future.
explanation:
A long-term study published by the Harvard Gazette found that, beyond exercise and diet, optimism (expecting good things in your future) was linked to longer life. That's close to how Greek lexicons define elpis, the word for hope: a confident expectation of good.

Jesus warned of a time when "men's hearts" would be "failing them from fear." If you feed constantly on end-time videos and alarming news without time in the Word, fear will grip your heart. Put on "the helmet of the hope of salvation." The world may grow darker, but your future is bright: the Lord is coming for His church.

text: Under the law, your value was set by your strength, and fell after sixty. If you were too poor, you went to the priest, and he set your value.
explanation:
God told Moses how to value people who made vows to Him: a man aged twenty to sixty, fifty shekels; over sixty, just fifteen. It's a valuation of natural strength: what you can do, measured by the law. Then comes a surprising verse: "If he is too poor to pay your valuation, then he shall present himself before the priest, and the priest shall set a value for him."

Moses represents the law, which can't come down to your level. The priest represents grace, which can. When you're too poor to measure up, you fall back into the arms of your High Priest, Jesus. Scripture doesn't even say what value the priest set. When grace sets your value, it's beyond the law's measure.

text: At ninety-nine, Abraham ran to the herd.
explanation:
When three visitors appeared at his tent, Abraham "ran to the herd" to prepare a meal. That was after he turned ninety-nine. Scripture doesn't claim he had a special body: Paul says it was "already dead," and Sarah was long past childbearing. Abraham didn't deny those facts. He simply "did not consider" them. He considered God's promise instead.

God had changed his name from Abram to Abraham, "father of many nations," before he had a son with Sarah. Every time someone called his name, he was saying what God said. Within a year, Isaac was born, and after Sarah's death Abraham married again and had more children. Faith doesn't ignore the natural. It rises above it.

text: "I am as strong this day as on the day Moses sent me. Now give me this mountain." Caleb was eighty-five.
explanation:
Caleb was forty when he spied out the land, and forty-five years later he said his strength for war was unchanged. He asked for Hebron, the mountain where the giant Anakim lived, and he drove them out. Notice how often he says "as He said": his confidence rested on God's word to him.

Psalm 103 says, "Forget not all His benefits": He forgives all your iniquities, heals all your diseases, redeems your life from destruction, crowns you with lovingkindness, and "satisfies your mouth with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle's." Don't forget any of them. Say them over yourself every day.

text: "I believed and therefore I spoke." If you keep saying, "I'm getting old," you believe it, and you'll have what you say.
explanation:
The spirit of faith works like this: believe and speak. That's how you received your greatest gift, salvation: "with the heart one believes… and with the mouth confession is made." The same spirit of faith appropriates healing, protection and renewed strength. Often the word must be in your mouth before it settles in your heart.

The Lord once told Joseph Prince, "Many people grow old because they complain." It's natural to find fault and unnatural to praise. In Greek, the word for grace, charis, is also the word for thanks. Learn the supernatural habit of thanksgiving. Instead of "I'm getting old and forgetful," say, "My youth is renewed like the eagle's."
